newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian privatisation chief joins Norilsk fray.
newsitem.headline: Russian privatisation chief joins Norilsk fray.

text.p: Russia's top privatisation official, State Property Committee head Alfred Kokh, added his weight on Tuesday to growing government opposition to the tender of a controlling stake in mining giant Norilsk Nickel.

Just minutes before a six-member commission convened a meeting which could once and for all settle the destiny of the troubled nickel and precious metals producer, Kokh urged them to postpone privatisation.

"Yes, Kokh instructed the state representatives in the commission to vote for delaying the sale," Kokh's press secretary Viktoria Vergelskaya told Reuters, adding he had not set a period for the postponement.

Kokh was the second senior government official to speak out against the tender, the winner of which is due to be named at around 5 p.m. Moscow time (1300 GMT) on Tuesday. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Monday called for the tender be suspended.

The final outcome of the commission's meeting is far from clear, despite the heavyweight attack on the sale. It has been criticised for being unfairly weighted in favour of Uneximbank -- one of only two bidders in the auction.

The state is represented at the meeting by officials from the Finance Ministry, the State Property Committee (Russia's privatisation ministry) and the Federal Property Fund, all of which are expected to vote for postponing the tender.
The other three members -- from RAO Norilsky Nikel, Uneximbank and tender organiser MFK Moscow Partners -- are all likely to vote for deciding on the winner as planned on Tuesday.
The decisive factor in the knife-edge contest appears to be which commission member chairs the meeting, because the chair gets the casting vote.
Uneximbank sources said that under normal practice, the chair would either go to the tender organiser, in this case a Uneximbank ally, or Uneximbank itself.

Uneximbank, Russia's third largest bank headed by formidable former first deputy prime minister Vladimir Potanin, won control of the 38 percent stake (representing 51 percent of voting shares) in a shares-for-loans swap with the state in 1995.
But the highly public row being played out in Russian media appears to pit Potanin against Chernomyrdin -- Russia's second most powerful politician.
Chernomyrdin has considerable leverage, given that the state officially owns the Norilsk stake.
He may also play the card of threatening to scupper Uneximbank's recent victory in Russia's biggest ever privatisation, the sale of 25 percent in Russian telecoms holding company Svyazinvest.
Uneximbank headed the winning $1.875-billion consortium, which itself caused unprecedented outrage.
Russian media, controlled by powerful tycoons who participants in the sale said belong to the losing consortium, slammed the Svyazinvest sale and demanded the conditions be reviewed.
But analysts dismissed the uproar as sour grapes, since the losers simply bid less than the Uneximbank group.
However, the Norilsk tender is seen as a much more obvious target for accusations of closed deals and unfair competition.
Uneximbank has said all along that foreign companies could not bid for the stake, drastically reducing the number of potential competitors.
Bank MFK (ICFI in English), linked to the tender organiser MFK-Moscow Partners, is also the investment arm of Uneximbank -- a link which has raised a few eyebrows in the domestic and foreign press.

Controversy surrounding the auction has cast doubt over RAO Norilsky Nikel's plans to double its share capital by issuing 126 million ordinary shares, and convert its existing preferred shares to voting ordinary stock.
News of the possible suspension of the auction caused the preferred shares, worth less than ordinaries, to fall sharply on Monday after rising on news of the conversion last week.
Norilsk is part of a round of state sell-offs, which in 1997 could raise between $4-5 billion for Russian state coffers.
